passage:
Monday: In the team huddle, Himani slid the draft proposal across the table. 'They'll reject it. The client always goes with the cheapest vendor, and we're not the cheapest.' Sarita, her manager, heard the certainty in her voice. 'Is that something you know, or a guess?' Himani hesitated. 'A guess. A strong one.' 'Then let's write it down and test it. How sure are you?' 'Ninety percent.'
Thursday: They sent the proposal with one extra page on after-sales support, Himani's idea.
The next Tuesday: The client called. No signature yet, but they wanted a second meeting about the support model. Sarita, who had privately expected a quick yes, was as surprised as Himani. 'Put it in the notebook,' Sarita said. 'Ninety percent no. Got: maybe.'

qa.q: How sure was Himani that the client would reject the proposal?
qa.a: Himani was ninety percent sure.

qa.q: What did Sarita notice in Himani's words, and why did it matter to Sarita?
qa.a: Sarita heard the certainty and felt concerned that a guess was being treated as fact, which could stop the team from trying at all.

qa.q: Which of Sarita's choices helped the team most, and why?
qa.a: Asking 'Is that something you know, or a guess?' and writing down a number turned a verdict into a test, and Himani's extra page came out of it.

qa.q: How might Himani feel after the client asked for a second meeting?
qa.a: Himani may feel surprised and a little hopeful 🙂, since a ninety percent no turned into a maybe, partly because of her own idea.

grounding: Shows a manager who hears an employee declare a client rejection certain, suggests testing it as a guess, and is surprised along with her by the result.

passage: Hrithik, you said 'they'll never go for it' three times in that meeting. Let me tell you about my first year as a team lead, at twenty-six. I had a designer, Mehrunissa, brilliant and gloomy. Before every pitch she'd say, 'Tejas, they'll reject it. Certainly.' And I was the opposite, sure of every yes. One day I said, 'Fine. You write your guess, I'll write mine, and we open them after.' It became a game. For a year we kept those slips in an old biscuit tin. Do you know the score? She was wrong more often than right, but so was I. The clients surprised both of us, again and again. What changed was that nobody on the team said 'certainly' any more without smiling.

qa.q: Where did Tejas and Mehrunissa keep their prediction slips?
qa.a: They kept the slips in an old biscuit tin.

qa.q: Why might Mehrunissa have said 'Certainly' before every pitch?
qa.a: Saying 'certainly' may have felt like protection: if rejection was already expected, it would hurt less when it came.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tejas's story, and how could Hrithik use it?
qa.a: Writing guesses down and opening them afterwards turned certainty into a game with a score; Hrithik could write 'they'll never go for it' with a number and check it after the next meeting.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have felt once 'certainly' came with a smile?
qa.a: The team probably felt lighter and freer to try ideas, because forecasts had become guesses to check instead of verdicts that ended the discussion.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling how, as a young team lead, they had a gloomy designer write predictions to test, and the clients surprised them both.

passage: The flight to Kolkata was delayed again, and Sunaina was reviewing the proposal on a laptop at eight percent battery when Vikas called. 'Honestly, ma'am, there's no point sending it tonight. They'll reject it. They told us last year our rates were high.' Around her, an announcement boomed about gate changes. Sunaina found a charging point behind a pillar and sat on the floor. 'Vikas, last year is one fact. Tonight's rejection is a guess. Want to test it?' 'How?' 'Send it with the new payment schedule, and write down what you expect. I'll write mine.' He laughed a little. 'Rejected.' She typed: 'Accepted, maybe after haggling.' Three days later the client wrote back. They wanted the project, but only half of it. Neither of them had seen that coming.

qa.q: How much battery did Sunaina's laptop have?
qa.a: Sunaina's laptop was at eight percent battery.

qa.q: What might Sunaina have been thinking when Vikas said there was no point sending it?
qa.a: Sunaina was likely concerned but hopeful, seeing that Vikas was treating one fact from last year as proof about tonight, and wanted to test that certainty instead.

qa.q: What made Sunaina's suggestion workable under pressure?
qa.a: Writing down two predictions took seconds, even on a dying laptop at an airport, and it kept the proposal moving instead of letting a guess stop it.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when the client wanted half the project?
qa.a: Vikas may feel surprised and a bit relieved that his 'rejected' was wrong, while noticing that Sunaina's hopeful guess was not quite right either.

grounding: Shows a manager stuck at an airport who hears an employee call a rejection certain and has them both write guesses, and the result surprises both.

passage:
At the small architecture firm in Chennai, Rakesh closed his laptop with a sigh. "They'll reject it. The client wants glass towers, and we've given them a courtyard house. I'd put money on it."

Deepak, his manager, pulled up a chair. Deepak privately thought the design was brilliant and was sure of a yes. "Okay. Is that something you know, or a guess?"

Rakesh paused. "A guess. A strong guess."

"Then let's test it. Write down your prediction. I'll write mine." Deepak folded a sticky note: "Yes, full design." Rakesh wrote: "Rejected outright."

On Friday the client called. They didn't want the courtyard house for their main site. But they loved the shaded verandas and asked the firm to design a small community library for their second plot.

Deepak laughed and stuck both notes on the board. "We were both wrong."

Rakesh looked at the notes for a long moment, then started a new folder: "Library".

qa.q: What did the client ask the firm to design for their second plot?
qa.a: A small community library.

qa.q: Why was Rakesh ready to "put money on" a rejection?
qa.a: Rakesh felt gloomy and certain, expecting the client to want glass towers; the forecast felt so sure that it seemed like knowledge, not a guess.

qa.q: What worked about Deepak's approach when Rakesh predicted a rejection?
qa.a: Deepak asked whether it was knowledge or a guess and turned it into a test, with both predictions written down. That made room for a real result instead of an argument about who was right.

qa.q: What does the outcome show Deepak about Deepak's own optimism?
qa.a: Deepak had been sure of a full yes and was wrong too. The result surprised both of them, a reminder that confident hope can miss just as gloomy prediction can.

grounding: A manager hears an employee say the client will certainly reject a design, suggests treating it as a guess to test, and the result surprises them both.

passage:
The warehouse office in Ludhiana smelled of cardboard and tea.

"Kiran ma'am, there's no point sending the canteen bid," Baljeet said. "The school will pick the bigger supplier. They always do."

Kiran looked up from the invoices. "Always?"

"Well. Every time I've heard of."

"How many times is that?"

He thought. "Two."

"So is it a fact or a forecast?"

"...A forecast."

"Good. Forecasts can be tested. Write yours down." She tore a page from her diary. "I'll write mine."

He wrote, "They'll say no." She wrote, "They'll say yes to all of it."

"And if you're wrong?" she asked.

"Then I'll bring the samosas."

Ten days later, the school's email arrived. They had accepted the fruit and milk supply, but not the snacks.

Baljeet read it twice. "Half yes."

Kiran grinned. "Half wrong, both of us. Samosas are on me."

qa.q: What did the school accept in the end?
qa.a: They had accepted the fruit and milk supply, but not the snacks.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet feel sure the school would pick the bigger supplier?
qa.a: Baljeet felt discouraged because he had heard of it happening twice and treated that as a rule, so the rejection felt certain rather than like a guess.

qa.q: Which question from Kiran started to change how Baljeet saw his prediction?
qa.a: "So is it a fact or a forecast?" It made him admit it was a guess, which opened the door to testing it instead of giving up on the bid.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel about her own prediction being half wrong?
qa.a: Kiran seems amused and honest about it, offering the samosas herself. It reminds her that her own optimism needs testing too, not just Baljeet's gloom.

grounding: A manager hears an employee insist a bid will be rejected, has them both write predictions, and the half-accepted result surprises both of them.
